1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable height-adjustable equipment platform supports a heavy machine above a roof, floor, vehicle bed, or other support surface while keeping the equipment deck parallel to a rectangular base frame. The base frame carries four upright guide towers, one near each corner. The equipment deck carries four corner posts that slide vertically in the respective guide towers. Each corner post has a rack along an inward-facing side. A pinion in each guide tower meshes with the rack of that corner post, so rotation of the pinion raises or lowers that corner of the deck.
6	
7	The two front pinions are fixed to a front transverse shaft and the two rear pinions are fixed to a rear transverse shaft. A sprocket on the front shaft, a sprocket on the rear shaft, and one endless synchronizing chain couple the shafts so all four pinions rotate together. A removable hand crank turns a worm input shaft. The worm input shaft drives a worm wheel fixed to the front transverse shaft. Turning the crank therefore raises or lowers all four corner posts by the same distance and prevents the deck from racking in the guide towers. The worm drive resists back-driving but is not the only load-holding feature.
8	
9	Each guide tower also carries a locking pawl that pivots between a locked position engaging the rack of its corner post and a released position clear of the rack. A compression spring biases each locking pawl toward the locked position. The four locking pawls are connected by four release cables to a release balance bar mounted on the base frame. A release handle pivots the balance bar. Pulling and holding the release handle tensions the four release cables and moves all four locking pawls clear of the racks. The balance bar can pivot slightly relative to the release handle so cable-length differences do not leave one pawl engaged while the other pawls are released. Releasing the handle lets the four pawl springs return the pawls into engagement with the nearest rack teeth. The deck load is then carried through the four engaged locking pawls and the guide towers rather than through the worm drive alone.
10	
11	Each locking pawl carries a locked-state flag that is visible through a window in the corresponding guide tower only when that pawl is fully engaged with a rack tooth. The operator must see all four flags before removing the hand crank or loading the deck. A mechanical interlock on the crank socket blocks insertion of the hand crank unless the release handle is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle until the crank is removed. This sequence prevents a pawl from being dragged across a rack tooth while the platform is being adjusted and prevents the platform from being left with the pawls released.
12	
13	To use the platform, the operator places the base frame on the support surface, mounts the equipment on the deck, pulls and holds the release handle, inserts and turns the hand crank until the desired deck height is reached, removes the hand crank, releases the handle, and confirms that all four locked-state flags are visible. The synchronized shafts keep the deck parallel to the base frame throughout the height change. For service, a removable cover gives access to the worm drive, sprockets, chain, pawls, and cable adjusters without removing the equipment deck.
14	
15	In supported variants, the endless chain is replaced by a toothed belt or a train of gears, the hand crank is replaced by a motor acting on the same worm input shaft, or the platform uses three or more than four guide towers with one rack, pinion, spring-biased pawl, release cable, and locked-state flag at each guided post. Turning the crank therefore raises or lowers all four corner posts by the same distance and prevents the deck from racking in the guide towers. The worm drive resists back-driving but is not the only load-holding feature.

Each guide tower also carries a locking pawl that pivots between a locked position engaging the rack of its corner post and a released position clear of the rack. The deck load is then carried through the four engaged locking pawls and the guide towers rather than through the worm drive alone.

In supported variants, the endless chain is replaced by a toothed belt or a train of gears, the hand crank is replaced by a motor acting on the same worm input shaft, or the platform uses three or more than four guide towers with one rack, pinion, spring-biased pawl, release cable, and locked-state flag at each guided post. input.content:
Heavy machines are frequently installed above the surface that carries them. A rooftop unit may have to stand clear of a membrane, a shop machine may have to stand clear of a wash-down floor, and equipment carried on a vehicle bed may have to stand clear of the bed itself. When the required standoff height is not known until the machine is in place, or when the height has to change later, a fixed pedestal or a stack of shims is inconvenient, because setting or resetting the height means lifting the machine off the support again.

A height-adjustable platform avoids that lifting, but it introduces three problems that have to be solved together before such a platform can be trusted under a heavy machine.

The first problem is parallelism. If each corner of a deck is adjusted through its own screw, jack, or shim stack, the corners are adjusted one after another. The deck twists and cocks in its guides while the adjustment is in progress, the guided members bind against their guides, and the finished height at one corner differs from the finished height at another, so that the machine is left out of level and the guides are left preloaded.

The second problem is load holding. A drive train that both moves the deck and holds it is a single load path. Its gearing, its fasteners, and its input coupling all have to carry the standing weight of the machine for as long as the machine is installed, and any wear, backlash, or maintenance operation on that drive train is a wear, backlash, or maintenance operation on the only thing supporting the load.

The third problem is the state of the locks. Where a platform is held by separate mechanical locks, those locks must be released to adjust the height and must be returned afterwards. Two failure modes follow. A lock that is only partly released is dragged across the toothed member it engages while the platform is being adjusted, which damages the tooth flanks it will later have to sit on, and a lock that is never returned leaves the platform standing on its drive train while looking, from the outside, exactly like a platform that is locked. Where several locks are pulled by one linkage through separate flexible connections, ordinary differences in connection length make the partly released condition the normal condition rather than the exception, because the shortest connection lifts its lock first and the longest connection may not lift its lock at all.

No prior-art search was performed for this application, and the references available during preparation of this application do not include any document. The art that bears on the following disclosure may therefore be incomplete. What follows is described on the basis of the inventor's own disclosure.

There remains a need for a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform that changes the height of every guided post of a deck by the same distance from a single input, that holds the resulting height through load locks that are independent of the drive train, that releases every one of those load locks together despite differences in the lengths of the flexible connections that pull them, and that shows the operator, before the platform is loaded, that every load lock has in fact returned.

A reusable height-adjustable equipment platform supports a machine above a support surface such as a roof, a floor, or a vehicle bed while keeping an equipment deck parallel to a base frame.

In one aspect, the platform comprises a base frame carrying a plurality of upright guide towers and an equipment deck carrying a like plurality of posts that slide vertically in the respective guide towers. Each post carries a rack, and each guide tower carries a pinion meshing with the rack of the post that slides in that guide tower, so that rotation of the pinion raises or lowers that post. A synchronizing transmission couples the pinions of all of the guide towers so that the pinions rotate together, and a rotary input drives the synchronizing transmission, whereby a single input rotation raises or lowers every post by the same distance and the deck does not rack in the guide towers.

In a further aspect, each guide tower carries a locking pawl mounted to pivot between a locked position engaging the rack of the post sliding in that guide tower and a released position clear of that rack, and a spring biases each locking pawl toward the locked position. The deck load at each post is carried through the engaged locking pawl and the guide tower rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone, so that the transmission is not the only load path under a standing machine.

In a further aspect, a release balance bar is mounted on the base frame and is connected to every locking pawl by a respective release cable, and a release handle pivots the release balance bar. Pulling and holding the release handle tensions all of the release cables together and moves all of the locking pawls to their released positions. The release balance bar is pivotable relative to the release handle so that differences in the effective lengths of the release cables are taken up by pivoting of the release balance bar and no locking pawl is left engaged with its rack while the remaining locking pawls are released. Releasing the release handle allows each spring to return its locking pawl into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack.

In a further aspect, each locking pawl carries a locked-state flag that is visible through a window in the corresponding guide tower only when that locking pawl is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack, so that the state of every load lock can be confirmed from outside the platform before the platform is loaded.

In a further aspect, a crank socket receives a removable hand crank that turns the rotary input, and a mechanical interlock associated with the crank socket blocks insertion of the hand crank into the crank socket unless the release handle is in its pulled position and blocks return of the release handle from its pulled position until the hand crank is removed from the crank socket. The interlock enforces an order of operations in which the locking pawls are clear of the racks before the platform can be driven and are returned to the racks only after the drive input has been disconnected, so that a locking pawl is neither dragged across a rack tooth during adjustment nor left released after adjustment.

In a further aspect, the rotary input comprises a worm input shaft and a worm wheel driven by the worm input shaft and fixed to a transverse shaft of the synchronizing transmission, the worm engagement resisting back-driving of the transmission by the deck load while the locking pawls carry that load.

In a further aspect, a method of adjusting the height of such a platform comprises pulling and holding the release handle to move all of the locking pawls clear of the racks, turning the rotary input to raise or lower all of the posts by the same distance while the deck remains parallel to the base frame, releasing the release handle so that each spring returns its locking pawl into engagement with the nearest tooth of its rack, and confirming that the locked-state flag of every locking pawl is visible through the window of the corresponding guide tower.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to a front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to a rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 is journalled in the base frame 10 and extends between the two guide towers 14 of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.

The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.

The release handle 52 acts on the release balance bar 48. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 together and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members of finite manufacturing tolerance whose effective lengths change with routing, wear, seating of the cable adjusters 62, and temperature. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across the teeth of its rack 18 as the platform was driven, damaging the very tooth flanks on which the load would afterwards stand, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

Crank and release interlock

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to a front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to a rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 is journalled in the base frame 10 and extends between the two guide towers 14 of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.

The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.

The release handle 52 acts on the release balance bar 48. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 together and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members of finite manufacturing tolerance whose effective lengths change with routing, wear, seating of the cable adjusters 62, and temperature. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across the teeth of its rack 18 as the platform was driven, damaging the very tooth flanks on which the load would afterwards stand, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The two members the operator handles are thus mutually exclusive by construction, and the failure modes of adjusting with the locks partly engaged and of leaving the platform standing with the locks released are removed rather than merely warned against.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

+A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

+The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. The release handle 52 cannot be allowed to return while the drive input is still connected, so the locking pawls 40 are not returned against moving racks 18. Conversely, once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return, and the operator who has finished the adjustment has nothing left to do that would keep the locking pawls 40 released. The two members the operator handles are thus mutually exclusive by construction, and the failure modes of adjusting with the locks partly engaged and of leaving the platform standing with the locks released are removed rather than merely warned against.
+Method of use

+In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

+When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.
+Further embodiments

+The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

+The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by either at different times, the crank socket 38 remaining available as a manual input.

+The platform is reusable. It can be lowered, unloaded, moved to another support surface 64, loaded again, and reset to a different height, and the members that carry the standing load, namely the locking pawls 40, the racks 18, the guide towers 14, and the base frame 10, are inspectable through the removable cover 60 and through the windows 56 between uses.

+The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Each post carries a rack and each guide tower carries a pinion meshing with that rack, and a synchronizing transmission couples the pinions so that one rotary input moves every post by the same distance and the deck stays parallel to the base frame. A spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower engages the rack of the post sliding in it, so the standing load passes through the engaged pawls and the guide towers rather than through the transmission. Release cables connect all of the pawls to a release balance bar that is pivoted by a release handle and is itself pivotable relative to the handle, so differences in cable length cannot leave one pawl engaged while the others are released. A locked-state flag on each pawl is visible through a window in its guide tower only when that pawl is fully engaged, and a mechanical interlock blocks insertion of a hand crank unless the handle is pulled and blocks return of the handle until the crank is removed.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to a front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to a rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 is journalled in the base frame 10 and extends between the two guide towers 14 of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.

The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.

The release handle 52 acts on the release balance bar 48. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 together and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members of finite manufacturing tolerance whose effective lengths change with routing, wear, seating of the cable adjusters 62, and temperature. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across the teeth of its rack 18 as the platform was driven, damaging the very tooth flanks on which the load would afterwards stand, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

Crank and release interlock

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. The release handle 52 cannot be allowed to return while the drive input is still connected, so the locking pawls 40 are not returned against moving racks 18. Conversely, once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return, and the operator who has finished the adjustment has nothing left to do that would keep the locking pawls 40 released. The two members the operator handles are thus mutually exclusive by construction, and the failure modes of adjusting with the locks partly engaged and of leaving the platform standing with the locks released are removed rather than merely warned against.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by either at different times, the crank socket 38 remaining available as a manual input.

The platform is reusable. It can be lowered, unloaded, moved to another support surface 64, loaded again, and reset to a different height, and the members that carry the standing load, namely the locking pawls 40, the racks 18, the guide towers 14, and the base frame 10, are inspectable through the removable cover 60 and through the windows 56 between uses.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

lines: A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

-The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

+The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

5:Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.
7:The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.
9:Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.
13:A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.
15:A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.
19:Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to a front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to a rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 is journalled in the base frame 10 and extends between the two guide towers 14 of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.
21:A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.
23:A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.
33:With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.
39:Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.
59:In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.
65:The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.
69:The platform is reusable. It can be lowered, unloaded, moved to another support surface 64, loaded again, and reset to a different height, and the members that carry the standing load, namely the locking pawls 40, the racks 18, the guide towers 14, and the base frame 10, are inspectable through the removable cover 60 and through the windows 56 between uses.
