The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to a front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to a rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 is journalled in the base frame 10 and extends between the two guide towers 14 of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.

The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.

The release handle 52 acts on the release balance bar 48. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 together and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members of finite manufacturing tolerance whose effective lengths change with routing, wear, seating of the cable adjusters 62, and temperature. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across the teeth of its rack 18 as the platform was driven, damaging the very tooth flanks on which the load would afterwards stand, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

Crank and release interlock

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. The release handle 52 cannot be allowed to return while the drive input is still connected, so the locking pawls 40 are not returned against moving racks 18. Conversely, once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return, and the operator who has finished the adjustment has nothing left to do that would keep the locking pawls 40 released. The two members the operator handles are thus mutually exclusive by construction, and the failure modes of adjusting with the locks partly engaged and of leaving the platform standing with the locks released are removed rather than merely warned against.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by either at different times, the crank socket 38 remaining available as a manual input.

The platform is reusable. It can be lowered, unloaded, moved to another support surface 64, loaded again, and reset to a different height, and the members that carry the standing load, namely the locking pawls 40, the racks 18, the guide towers 14, and the base frame 10, are inspectable through the removable cover 60 and through the windows 56 between uses.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

A front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32 are journalled in the base frame 10, within the space that the removable cover 60 closes.

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends between the two guide towers of its side, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

Crank and release interlock

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine that is to be supported, for example through mounting holes, rails, or clamps at the upper face of the equipment deck 12, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14, so that the four guide towers 14 together restrain the equipment deck 12 against horizontal displacement and against tilting, and leave it free to move vertically. Each guide tower 14 is a hollow upright member whose interior corresponds to the cross section of the corner post 16 that slides in it, and bearing surfaces at the upper and lower ends of the interior of the guide tower 14 take the horizontal reactions produced by an off-centre machine on the equipment deck 12.

Each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10. Placing the rack 18 on the inward-facing side keeps the toothed face of the rack 18 and the members that engage it inside the footprint of the platform, where they are shielded from weather and from impact, and allows the drive members of all four guide towers 14 to be reached from within the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 so that the mesh with the rack 18 is maintained over the whole travel of the corner post 16.

A removable cover 60 closes the base frame 10 over the drive members and the release members described below. Removing the removable cover 60 gives access to the worm drive, the sprockets, the synchronizing chain, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters for inspection, lubrication, and adjustment without removing the equipment deck 12 and without taking the machine off the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 projects from the base frame 10 where an operator standing beside the platform can reach it, and a hand crank 36 is inserted into the base frame 10 at the same side to drive the platform. The release handle 52 and the hand crank 36 are the only two members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

A front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32 are journalled in the base frame 10, within the space that the removable cover 60 closes.

Referring to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it necessarily rotate through the same angle.

A front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 have the same number of teeth, so that the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 also rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together and all four racks 18 have the same pitch, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the corner posts 16 do not cock in the guide towers 14. The equipment deck 12 is therefore not racked in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

A worm input shaft 32 is journalled in the base frame 10 and carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 is a high-reduction mesh that resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12, so that the equipment deck 12 does not run down when the input torque is removed and the operator can let go of the input at any point in the travel. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are relieved of the standing load and are loaded only while the height is being changed.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32, as shown in FIG. 4. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34 and producing the same synchronized travel of the four corner posts 16.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together, and the parallel travel of the equipment deck 12 follows from that constraint rather than from the skill of the operator.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 3, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which a tooth of the locking pawl 40 lies between two teeth of the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14 and bears on the flank of a rack tooth, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 seated between the guide tower 14 and the locking pawl 40 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that each of the four load paths stands alone and none of them passes through the synchronizing transmission. The standing load of the machine therefore does not rest on the worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, or the input coupling, and the drive members can be inspected, lubricated, or adjusted through the removable cover 60 while the machine remains on the loaded equipment deck 12.

The tooth pitch of the rack 18 sets the increments at which the locking pawls 40 can engage. Because the four racks 18 are driven through a common synchronizing transmission, the four locking pawls 40 arrive at corresponding positions relative to their respective racks 18, and all four engage teeth at the same height rather than at heights that differ by a pitch from corner to corner.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 4, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10 on a balance bar pivot 50, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to the locking pawl 40 of one guide tower 14 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 in each release cable 46 sets the free length of that release cable 46, and all four cable adjusters 62 are reachable through the removable cover 60.

The release handle 52 acts on the release balance bar 48. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 together and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members of finite manufacturing tolerance whose effective lengths change with routing, wear, seating of the cable adjusters 62, and temperature. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across the teeth of its rack 18 as the platform was driven, damaging the very tooth flanks on which the load would afterwards stand, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, and the platform cannot be left unlocked by the omission of a locking step, because locking is the unpowered rest state of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 3. When the locking pawl 40 is in its released position, or is held short of full engagement because its tooth has landed on the crest of a rack tooth, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48, either of which can be at rest while a locking pawl 40 stands unengaged.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before the machine on the equipment deck 12 is put into service. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated, and the operator restores engagement by turning the hand crank 36 a small amount so that the corner posts 16 move to the next tooth position and the compression springs 44 seat all four locking pawls 40.

Crank and release interlock

A mechanical interlock 58 associated with the crank socket 38 couples the crank socket 38 to the release handle 52, as shown in FIG. 4. The mechanical interlock 58 comprises a member that is displaced by the release handle 52 and that lies in the mouth of the crank socket 38 when the release handle 52 is in its rest position, so that the hand crank 36 cannot be inserted into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position. The same member is captured by the shank of the hand crank 36 while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so that the release handle 52 cannot return from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged along a rack 18 during a height change. The release handle 52 cannot be allowed to return while the drive input is still connected, so the locking pawls 40 are not returned against moving racks 18. Conversely, once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return, and the operator who has finished the adjustment has nothing left to do that would keep the locking pawls 40 released. The two members the operator handles are thus mutually exclusive by construction, and the failure modes of adjusting with the locks partly engaged and of leaving the platform standing with the locks released are removed rather than merely warned against.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which pivots the release balance bar 48 about the balance bar pivot 50, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 permits the hand crank 36 to be inserted into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from a rectangular equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by either at different times, the crank socket 38 remaining available as a manual input.

The platform is reusable. It can be lowered, unloaded, moved to another support surface 64, loaded again, and reset to a different height, and the members that carry the standing load, namely the locking pawls 40, the racks 18, the guide towers 14, and the base frame 10, are inspectable through the removable cover 60 and through the windows 56 between uses.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

# FIG. 1

## View

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from slightly above and from the front left, so that the front side and the left side are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on all visible sides.

A base frame 10 rests on the upper face of the support surface 64. The base frame 10 is a closed rectangular frame drawn as a low box in perspective, longer from left to right than from front to back, with its front wall and left wall visible as solid faces.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each corner of the base frame 10. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow rectangular column of the same height, standing vertically with its lower end joined to the base frame 10. The two rear guide towers 14 are partly occluded by the two front guide towers 14.

An equipment deck 12 is a flat rectangular slab of the same plan outline as the base frame 10, held above the upper ends of the guide towers 14 and parallel to the base frame 10. Its upper face is empty.

Four corner posts 16 depend from the four corners of the underside of the equipment deck 12 and run vertically down into the four guide towers 14. Each corner post 16 is a straight square-section column, visible over the open gap between the underside of the equipment deck 12 and the upper end of the guide tower 14 it enters, and occluded below that upper end by the wall of the guide tower 14.

A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel lying flat against the front wall of the base frame 10, between the two front guide towers 14 and inset from both of them, shown schematically.

A release handle 52 is an elongated straight lever projecting forward and slightly upward from the front wall of the base frame 10, to the left of the removable cover 60, its inner end meeting that wall and its outer end free, shown schematically.

A hand crank 36 is drawn to the right of the removable cover 60 as a short horizontal shaft entering the front wall of the base frame 10, a radial arm at the outer end of that shaft, and a short grip parallel to the shaft at the far end of the radial arm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

10, 12, 14, 16, 36, 52, 60, 64

## Numeral placement

Point 64 well inside the exposed slab in front of the platform. Point 10 well inside the visible front wall of the frame box, away from the panel and the two projecting members. Point 12 well inside the visible upper face of the deck slab. Point 14 well inside the outer face of the front left column. Point 16 well inside the exposed length of the front left post. Point 60 well inside the panel. Point 52 well inside the projecting lever. Point 36 at the radial arm of the crank.

# FIG. 2

## View

A schematic plan view, looking straight down on the synchronized drive with the deck and the cover omitted, so that the shafts, the toothed wheels, and the chain loop lie in the plane of the drawing. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A plain rectangular boundary outline, wider than it is tall, occupies most of the drawing area and represents the frame that carries the drive, shown schematically. A small unnumbered square block sits at each of its four inner corners.

A front transverse shaft 22 is a straight horizontal line of uniform thickness running left to right across the lower part of the boundary outline, its two ends reaching the two lower square blocks.

# FIG. 3

## View

An enlarged fragmentary vertical sectional view through one guide tower and the corner post that slides in it, cut on a vertical plane passing through the locking pawl of that guide tower, the locking pawl being shown in its locked position. Sectioned solids carry hatching. A short irregular break line closes the upper end and another closes the lower end of the fragment, both well inside the drawing area and clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A guide tower 14 appears in section as two upright hatched wall bands of equal thickness, a left wall band and a right wall band, running between the break lines and spaced apart across the drawing area.

A corner post 16 appears in section as an upright hatched column standing between the two wall bands and running between the break lines. Its left side lies close to the inner face of the left wall band with a narrow clearance. A wider open gap is left between its right side and the inner face of the right wall band.

A rack 18 is a row of uniform triangular teeth of constant pitch along the right side of the corner post 16, the tooth points directed right into the wider gap, the row running the full sectioned length of the corner post 16.

A locking pawl 40 is a solid unhatched body in the wider gap at mid height of the fragment. Its left end is a single tooth whose point lies in a valley between two teeth of the rack 18 and rests against the lower flank of the tooth above it. The body widens from that tooth toward the right.

A pawl pivot 42 is a small circle with a centre mark within the right-hand part of the body of the locking pawl 40, carried by a short bracket joining the inner face of the right wall band, so that the locking pawl 40 is free to swing about the circle.

A compression spring 44 is a coiled line in the wider gap below the pawl pivot 42, its right end seated against the inner face of the right wall band and its left end seated against the lower right portion of the body of the locking pawl 40.

A locked-state flag 54 is a small tab projecting right from the upper part of the body of the locking pawl 40, above the pawl pivot 42, its right end reaching into the thickness of the right wall band.

A window 56 is a rectangular opening through the right wall band, drawn as an unhatched break in that band bounded by a short horizontal line above and a short horizontal line below. The window 56 is at the height of the locked-state flag 54, and the right end of the locked-state flag 54 is visible in the opening.

## Numerals on this sheet

14, 16, 18, 40, 42, 44, 54, 56

## Numeral placement

Point 14 well inside the hatching of the left wall band. Point 16 well inside the hatching of the column between the wall bands. Point 18 at the row of triangular teeth above the locking pawl 40. Point 40 well inside the widened part of the unhatched body. Point 42 at the small circle within that body. Point 44 at the coiled line below that circle. Point 54 at the tab projecting right from that body. Point 56 at the unhatched opening in the right wall band.

Four locking pawls 40 are four small rectangular blocks, one near each corner of the drawing area, shown schematically.

A balance bar pivot 50 is a small circle with a centre mark at the middle of the release balance bar 48, drawn where the release balance bar 48 crosses the upper end of the release handle 52, so that the bar and the handle turn on the same circle relative to one another.

A release handle 52 is a straight lever running from the balance bar pivot 50 downward to the lower part of the drawing area, ending in a short cross grip at its lower end.

A cable adjuster 62 is drawn in each of the four curved paths as a short barrel shape interrupting the path, each barrel on the outer part of its path between the release balance bar 48 and the block that path reaches.

A crank socket 38 is drawn to the right of the release handle 52 in the lower part of the drawing area as a short open-ended sleeve seen from the side, its open mouth facing downward and its closed end upward, shown schematically.

A mechanical interlock 58 is a small bar lying across the open mouth of the crank socket 38, together with a straight link line joining that small bar to the release handle 52 below the balance bar pivot 50, so that movement of the release handle 52 carries the small bar out of and into the open mouth.

38, 40, 46, 48, 50, 52, 58, 62

Point 40 well inside the block near the upper left corner. Point 48 well inside the elongated horizontal bar, left of its middle circle. Point 50 at that circle. # FIG. 1

## View

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from slightly above and from the front left, so that the front side and the left side are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on all visible sides.

A base frame 10 rests on the upper face of the support surface 64. The base frame 10 is a closed rectangular frame drawn as a low box in perspective, longer from left to right than from front to back, with its front wall and left wall visible as solid faces.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each corner of the base frame 10. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow rectangular column of the same height, standing vertically with its lower end joined to the base frame 10. The two rear guide towers 14 are partly occluded by the two front guide towers 14.

An equipment deck 12 is a flat rectangular slab of the same plan outline as the base frame 10, held above the upper ends of the guide towers 14 and parallel to the base frame 10. Its upper face is empty.

Four corner posts 16 depend from the four corners of the underside of the equipment deck 12 and run vertically down into the four guide towers 14. Each corner post 16 is a straight square-section column, visible over the open gap between the underside of the equipment deck 12 and the upper end of the guide tower 14 it enters, and occluded below that upper end by the wall of the guide tower 14.

A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel lying flat against the front wall of the base frame 10, between the two front guide towers 14 and inset from both of them, shown schematically.

A release handle 52 is an elongated straight lever projecting forward and slightly upward from the front wall of the base frame 10, to the left of the removable cover 60, its inner end meeting that wall and its outer end free, shown schematically.

A hand crank 36 is drawn to the right of the removable cover 60 as a short horizontal shaft entering the front wall of the base frame 10, a radial arm at the outer end of that shaft, and a short grip parallel to the shaft at the far end of the radial arm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

10, 12, 14, 16, 36, 52, 60, 64

## Numeral placement

Point 64 well inside the exposed slab in front of the platform. Point 10 well inside the visible front wall of the frame box, away from the panel and the two projecting members. Point 12 well inside the visible upper face of the deck slab. Point 14 well inside the outer face of the front left column. Point 16 well inside the exposed length of the front left post. Point 60 well inside the panel. Point 52 well inside the projecting lever. Point 36 at the radial arm of the crank.

# FIG. 2

## View

A schematic plan view, looking straight down on the synchronized drive with the deck and the cover omitted, so that the shafts, the toothed wheels, and the chain loop lie in the plane of the drawing. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A plain rectangular boundary outline, wider than it is tall, occupies most of the drawing area and represents the frame that carries the drive, shown schematically. A small unnumbered square block sits at each of its four inner corners.

A front transverse shaft 22 is a straight horizontal line of uniform thickness running left to right across the lower part of the boundary outline, its two ends reaching the two lower square blocks.

A rear transverse shaft 24 is a straight horizontal line of the same thickness running left to right across the upper part of the boundary outline, its two ends reaching the two upper square blocks.

Four pinions 20 are small toothed circles, one at each end of the front transverse shaft 22 and one at each end of the rear transverse shaft 24. Each toothed circle is centred on the shaft it belongs to and its teeth touch the nearer side of the adjacent square block.

A front sprocket 26 is a toothed circle larger than a pinion 20, centred on the front transverse shaft 22 to the left of the middle of that shaft.

A rear sprocket 28 is a toothed circle of the same size as the front sprocket 26, centred on the rear transverse shaft 24 directly above the front sprocket 26.

An endless synchronizing chain 30 is one closed loop path drawn around the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28, running along the outside of both toothed circles with a straight vertical run on the left of the pair and a straight vertical run on the right of the pair.

A worm wheel 34 is a toothed circle larger than a pinion 20, centred on the front transverse shaft 22 to the right of the middle of that shaft.

A worm input shaft 32 is a straight vertical line running from the worm wheel 34 downward across the lower side of the boundary outline, its lower end free outside that outline. A short barrel shape on the worm input shaft 32, at the end nearer the worm wheel 34, meets the toothed edge of the worm wheel 34 and represents the worm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34

## Numeral placement

Point 22 at the lower shaft line between the front sprocket 26 and the left pinion 20. Point 24 at the upper shaft line between the rear sprocket 28 and the left pinion 20. Point 20 at the toothed circle at the right end of the lower shaft. Point 26 well inside the lower of the two chain-driven circles. Point 28 well inside the upper of the two chain-driven circles. Point 30 at the straight right-hand run of the closed loop path. Point 34 well inside the toothed circle on the right-hand part of the lower shaft. Point 32 at the vertical line below the boundary outline.

# FIG. 1

## View

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from above and from the front left, so that the front and left sides are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on all visible sides.

A base frame 10 rests on the upper face of the support surface 64. The base frame 10 is a closed rectangular frame drawn as a low box in perspective, longer from left to right than from front to back, with its front wall and left wall visible as solid faces.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each of its corners. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow rectangular column of the same height, standing vertically with its lower end joined to the base frame 10. The two rear guide towers 14 are partly occluded by the two front ones.

An equipment deck 12 is a flat rectangular slab of the same plan outline as the base frame 10, held above the upper ends of the guide towers 14 and parallel to the base frame 10. Its upper face is empty.

Four corner posts 16 depend from the corners of the underside of the equipment deck 12 and run vertically down into the four guide towers 14. Each corner post 16 is a straight square-section column, visible over the open gap between the deck underside and the upper end of the guide tower 14 it enters, and occluded below that upper end by the wall of the guide tower 14.

A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel lying flat against the front wall of the base frame 10, between the two front guide towers 14 and inset from both, shown schematically.

A release handle 52 is an elongated straight lever projecting forward and slightly upward from the front wall of the base frame 10, left of the removable cover 60, its inner end meeting that wall and its outer end free, shown schematically.

A hand crank 36 is drawn right of the removable cover 60 as a short horizontal shaft entering the front wall of the base frame 10, a radial arm at the outer end of that shaft, and a short grip parallel to the shaft at the far end of the arm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

10, 12, 14, 16, 36, 52, 60, 64

## Numeral placement

Point 64 well inside the exposed slab in front of the platform. Point 10 well inside the front wall of the frame box, away from the panel and the projecting members. Point 12 well inside the upper face of the deck slab. Point 14 well inside the outer face of the front left column. Point 16 well inside the exposed length of the front left post. Point 60 well inside the panel. Point 52 well inside the lever. Point 36 at the radial arm.

An enlarged fragmentary vertical sectional view through one guide tower and the corner post that slides in it, cut on a vertical plane passing through the locking pawl of that guide tower, the locking pawl being shown in its locked position. A guide tower 14 appears in section as two upright hatched wall bands of equal thickness, a left wall band and a right wall band, running between the break lines and spaced apart across the drawing area.

A corner post 16 appears in section as an upright hatched column standing between the two wall bands and running between the break lines. Its left side lies close to the inner face of the left wall band with a narrow clearance. A wider open gap is left between its right side and the inner face of the right wall band.

A rack 18 is a row of uniform triangular teeth of constant pitch along the right side of the corner post 16, the tooth points directed right into the wider gap, the row running the full sectioned length of the corner post 16.

A locking pawl 40 is a solid unhatched body in the wider gap at mid height of the fragment. Its left end is a single tooth whose point lies in a valley between two teeth of the rack 18 and rests against the lower flank of the tooth above it. The body widens from that tooth toward the right.

A pawl pivot 42 is a small circle with a centre mark within the right-hand part of the body of the locking pawl 40, carried by a short bracket joining the inner face of the right wall band, so that the locking pawl 40 is free to swing about the circle.

A compression spring 44 is a coiled line in the wider gap below the pawl pivot 42, its right end seated against the inner face of the right wall band and its left end seated against the lower right portion of the body of the locking pawl 40.

A locked-state flag 54 is a small tab projecting right from the upper part of the body of the locking pawl 40, above the pawl pivot 42, its right end reaching into the thickness of the right wall band.

A window 56 is a rectangular opening through the right wall band, drawn as an unhatched break in that band bounded by a short horizontal line above and a short horizontal line below. The window 56 is at the height of the locked-state flag 54, and the right end of the locked-state flag 54 is visible in the opening.

14, 16, 18, 40, 42, 44, 54, 56

Point 14 well inside the hatching of the left wall band. Point 16 well inside the hatching of the column between the wall bands. Point 18 at the row of triangular teeth above the locking pawl 40. # FIG. 1

## View

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from above and from the front left, so that the front and left sides are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on all visible sides.

A base frame 10 rests on the upper face of the support surface 64. It is a closed rectangular frame drawn as a low box in perspective, longer from left to right than from front to back, its front and left walls visible as solid faces.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each of its corners. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow rectangular column of the same height, standing vertically with its lower end joined to the base frame 10. The two rear guide towers 14 are partly occluded by the two front ones.

An equipment deck 12 is a flat rectangular slab of the same plan outline as the base frame 10, held above the upper ends of the guide towers 14 and parallel to the base frame 10. Its upper face is empty.

Four corner posts 16 depend from the corners of the underside of the equipment deck 12 and run vertically down into the four guide towers 14. Each corner post 16 is a straight square-section column, visible over the open gap between the deck underside and the upper end of the guide tower 14 it enters, and occluded below that upper end by the wall of the guide tower 14.

A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel lying flat against the front wall of the base frame 10, between the two front guide towers 14 and inset from both, shown schematically.

A release handle 52 is an elongated straight lever projecting forward and slightly upward from the front wall of the base frame 10, left of the removable cover 60, its inner end meeting that wall and its outer end free, shown schematically.

A hand crank 36 is drawn right of the removable cover 60 as a short horizontal shaft entering the front wall of the base frame 10, a radial arm at the outer end of that shaft, and a short grip parallel to the shaft at the far end of the arm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

10, 12, 14, 16, 36, 52, 60, 64

## Numeral placement

Point 64 well inside the exposed slab in front of the platform. Point 10 well inside the front wall of the frame box, away from the panel and the projecting members. Point 12 well inside the upper face of the deck slab. Point 14 well inside the outer face of the front left column. Point 16 well inside the exposed length of the front left post. Point 60 well inside the panel. Point 52 well inside the lever. Point 36 at the radial arm.

# FIG. 2

## View

A schematic plan view, looking straight down on the synchronized drive with the deck and the cover omitted, so that the shafts, toothed wheels, and chain loop lie in the plane of the drawing. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

## Structures and relationships

A plain rectangular boundary outline, wider than tall, occupies most of the drawing area and represents the frame carrying the drive, shown schematically. A small unnumbered square block sits at each of its four inner corners.

A front transverse shaft 22 is a straight horizontal line of uniform thickness running left to right across the lower part of the boundary outline, its ends reaching the two lower square blocks.

A rear transverse shaft 24 is a straight horizontal line of the same thickness running left to right across the upper part of the boundary outline, its ends reaching the two upper square blocks.

Four pinions 20 are small toothed circles, one at each end of the front transverse shaft 22 and one at each end of the rear transverse shaft 24. Each is centred on the shaft it belongs to and its teeth touch the nearer side of the adjacent square block.

A front sprocket 26 is a toothed circle larger than a pinion 20, centred on the front transverse shaft 22 to the left of the middle of that shaft.

A rear sprocket 28 is a toothed circle of the same size as the front sprocket 26, centred on the rear transverse shaft 24 directly above the front sprocket 26.

An endless synchronizing chain 30 is one closed loop path drawn around the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28, running along the outside of both circles with a straight vertical run on the left of the pair and another on the right of the pair.

A worm wheel 34 is a toothed circle larger than a pinion 20, centred on the front transverse shaft 22 to the right of the middle of that shaft.

A worm input shaft 32 is a straight vertical line running from the worm wheel 34 downward across the lower side of the boundary outline, its lower end free outside that outline. A short barrel shape on the worm input shaft 32, at the end nearer the worm wheel 34, meets the toothed edge of the worm wheel 34 and represents the worm, shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet

20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34

## Numeral placement

Point 22 at the lower shaft line left of the front sprocket 26. Point 24 at the upper shaft line left of the rear sprocket 28. Point 20 at the toothed circle at the right end of the lower shaft. Point 26 well inside the lower chain-driven circle. Point 28 well inside the upper chain-driven circle. Point 30 at the straight right-hand run of the loop path. Point 34 well inside the toothed circle on the right-hand part of the lower shaft. Point 32 at the vertical line below the boundary outline.

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from above and from the front left, so that the front and left sides are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on the visible sides.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each of its corners. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow rectangular column of the same height, standing vertically with its lower end joined to the base frame 10.
