The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it. Each pinion 20 is journalled in the guide tower 14 in mesh with the rack 18.

A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission.

The synchronizing transmission couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only load-holding features under a standing machine.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the input coupling remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in each release cable 46.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

The operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56 before removing the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38 and before loading the equipment deck 12. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which displaces the release balance bar 48, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 no longer blocks the crank socket 38, and the operator inserts the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from the equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: Every finding is corrected by conforming the text to the disclosure. The load-path statements now say the standing load is carried through the engaged locking pawls and the guide towers rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone, in claim 13, in both description passages, and in the abstract. The cable adjuster is recited without a function in claim 10 and the description. The removable cover is recited only as giving access on removal, in claim 11 and the description, and the enclosed-volume language is gone. The shafts are no longer journalled in the base frame in claims 4 and 5 or the description, and the parallel pinion journalling sentence went with it. Numeral 50 now has a single referent, the pivot connection between the release handle and the release balance bar, with the bar's mounting to the base frame carried on a separate support in both the description and FIG. 5, so the handle can displace the bar and the equalizing freedom has a joint to occur in. The rack tooth pitch sentence is deleted and the equipment deck is no longer called rectangular in the description. FIG. 4 is now taken on line 4-4 of FIG. 2, with a broken cutting-plane line, both endpoints, alignment, both arrow directions and the repeated designation specified in the FIG. 2 brief and the same designation used in the Brief Description and the FIG. 4 brief. The numeral table is unchanged, the abstract is 147 words, and every figure brief is well under the character limit.
reasoning: The exclusive load path was the most consequential fix because it reached claim 13. The disclosure says the worm drive is not the only load-holding feature and that the load is carried by the pawls and towers rather than through the worm drive alone, which is a shared-path statement. Claim 13 now recites 'rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone', which keeps the limitation that matters, the load reaching ground through the pawl, its pivot, the tower and the frame, without asserting that the transmission carries none of it. The description and abstract were brought to the same formulation so the three read consistently.

Claim 10 lost the cable adjuster's function rather than the adjuster itself. The adjuster is disclosed by name as a serviceable item, so it can be claimed as a structure in each release cable; what it sets is not disclosed. The method claim about adjusting a cable adjuster and the FIG. 5 barrel shape still stand on that same disclosed naming.

The cover finding had two halves, and the enclosure half also conflicted with the rest of the draft: each locking pawl sits in an upright guide tower, so a cover closing the base frame could not close over the pawls. Reciting only access on removal fixes the untraced geometry and the internal inconsistency at once, and the shafts no longer sit 'within the space that the removable cover closes'.

For numeral 50 I kept the joint the invention actually needs and moved the other one to an unnumbered support. The handle acts on the bar at pivot 50 and the bar turns slightly relative to the handle about that same circle, which is exactly the equalizing freedom the disclosure describes; the bar's attachment to the base frame is now a separate support spaced along the bar, so pulling the handle can displace the bar and tension all four cables. Claim 1 and claim 15 already recited the mounting and the relative pivoting as two things, so no claim needed amending, and FIG. 5 now depicts both.

The shaft mounting came out of claims 4 and 5 without weakening them, because what those claims are for is the two-shaft split of the pinions plus the chain form or the belt and gear-train form of the transmission; where the shafts are borne adds nothing to that and was not disclosed. I removed the pinion journalling sentence from the description for the same reason, since the disclosed relationship, a pinion in each guide tower meshing that tower's rack, is already stated in the preceding sentence.

The tooth pitch sentence was deleted outright rather than softened, because nothing in the text or claims depended on it and any weaker version would still assert a relationship between pitch and achievable heights that the disclosure never draws.

For the section line I used a single repeated designation 4-4 and put the full cutting-plane specification in the source view, FIG. 2: a broken straight line on a vertical plane containing the rack of the lower left corner post, both endpoints identified, the line running horizontally across that guide tower and the post within it, an arrow at each endpoint pointing toward the upper side of the drawing area, and the designation at both ends. The Brief Description and the FIG. 4 brief now name the same line, so the three can be checked against one another. The designation is drawing annotation and was not added to the numeral table or to any figure's numeral list.

content.content:
1	A height-adjustable equipment platform has a base frame carrying upright guide towers and an equipment deck carrying posts sliding in those guide towers. Each post carries a rack, each guide tower carries a pinion meshing with that rack, and a synchronizing transmission couples the pinions so one rotary input moves every post equally and the deck stays parallel to the base frame. A spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower engages the rack of the post sliding in it, so the standing load passes through the engaged pawls and the guide towers rather than through the transmission alone. Release cables connect the pawls to a release balance bar pivoted by a release handle and itself pivotable relative to that handle, so cable-length differences cannot leave one pawl engaged while the others release. A locked-state flag shows through a window of its guide tower only at full engagement.

input.answer:
The abstract now complies with 37 CFR 1.72(b) under either word-counting rule.

The overage came from hyphenated compounds being counted as two words each, which turned a plain count of 147 into the reported 151. The abstract is now 139 plain words and 143 with every hyphenated compound split, so it clears 150 with margin.

It still recites, in one paragraph: the base frame carrying upright guide towers with the equipment deck carrying posts sliding in them; a rack on each post and a pinion in each tower meshing it, coupled by a synchronizing transmission so one rotary input moves every post equally and the deck stays parallel to the base frame; a spring-biased locking pawl in each tower engaging the rack of the post sliding in it, so the standing load passes through the engaged pawls and the towers rather than through the transmission alone; release cables joining the pawls to a release balance bar pivoted by a release handle and itself pivotable relative to it, so cable-length differences cannot leave one pawl engaged while the others release; and a locked-state flag showing through a window of its tower only at full engagement.

No other file was modified. The 21 claims, the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Detailed Description, and the six figure briefs are untouched and remain synchronized, with FIG. 4 taken on line 4-4 of FIG. 2 and every sheet carrying eight or fewer numerals.

42	- **[major] FIG. 2 section line 4-4 and FIG. 4 place the rack on a post face that the transverse-shaft pinion cannot mesh with** (figures/FIG-2.md (section line 4-4 sentence and rack sentence); figures/FIG-4.md (rack sentence); draft/08-detailed-desc) - FIG. 2 draws section line 4-4 as a horizontal (transverse) broken line across the lower left guide tower, and FIG. 4, taken on that line, shows the rack teeth on the side of the corner post facing the right wall band. With the viewing arrows pointing toward the upper side of FIG. 2, the right of the FIG. 4 view is the transverse (left-right) direction of the platform, so the two briefs together assert that each rack faces along the transverse-shaft axis. A pinion fixed to the front or rear transverse shaft rotates about that same transverse axis; its teeth move in a plane perpendicular to that axis and can only mesh with a rack whose teeth face fore-and-aft. The disclosed arrangement therefore requires each rack to lie on the fore-or-aft inward-facing side of its corner post, and the cutting plane for FIG. 4 must run front-to-rear, not transversely. This is a contact-topology assertion about a functional toothed face, so it is substantive even though both views are labelled schematic. FIG. 2 also draws the pinion as a toothed circle in the plane of a plan view, which implies a vertical pinion axis and compounds the same conflict.
43	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-2.md, replace the rack sentence with: "A rack 18 is drawn on the side of each corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10 in the front-to-rear direction, that is, on the rear-facing side of each of the two lower corner posts 16 and on the front-facing side of each of the two upper corner posts 16, as a short row of teeth of constant pitch, the teeth shown schematically." Replace the section-line sentence with: "A section line 4-4 is drawn as a broken straight line lying on a vertical cutting plane perpendicular to the rack 18 of the lower left corner post 16, the broken line running from front to rear across the lower left guide tower 14 and the corner post 16 within it, its lower endpoint in the open area outside the base frame 10 in front of that guide tower and its upper endpoint inside the base frame 10 behind that guide tower, with an arrow at each of the two endpoints pointing toward the left side of the drawing area to give the viewing direction and the designation 4-4 placed at both endpoints." Leave figures/FIG-4.md unchanged; with this viewing direction its right wall band is the interior-facing wall of the guide tower and its rack orientation becomes correct.

Elsewhere the same document states that the pawls are held released while the handle is pulled, that the interlock blocks return of the handle until the crank is removed, and that the springs seat the pawls only "[o]nce the hand crank 36 has been removed". No flag can therefore be visible while the crank is still in the socket. The method paragraph and claim 18 both place the confirmation after the handle is released, so the sentence contradicts the rest of the application. The inventor's operating sequence supplies the consistent order.
45	  - Suggested fix: Replace the sentence with: "After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56."

Claims 2 and 16 recite a worm wheel "fixed to a transverse shaft of the synchronizing transmission", treating the shafts as part of the transmission, while claims 4 and 5 recite the front and rear transverse shafts as separately "further comprising" elements outside it. The same term therefore carries two different scopes across the claims and description.
47	  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md replace the definition sentence with: "The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together." The inventor states only that the load is carried through the engaged pawls and the guide towers; the pivot is never identified as a load-carrying member. Whether a pawl transmits load through its pivot pin or through a seat in the tower is a design assertion, not an inherent consequence of a pawl that pivots. No affirmative passage in the disclosure or conversation places the load path through the pivot.

The disclosure says only that a removable cover gives service access to the listed parts without removing the deck; it never states what the cover is mounted on or where along the platform it sits. The claim recitation is invention text, so the untraced mounting relationship must come out; the figure's relative placement between two named towers likewise conveys location rather than a bare depiction convention.
51	  - Suggested fix: In claim 21 replace "removing a removable cover from the base frame" with "removing a removable cover of the platform". In figures/FIG-1.md replace the cover sentence with: "A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel on a wall of the platform below the equipment deck 12, shown schematically."

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.
A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle. The front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission.

The synchronizing transmission couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only load-holding features under a standing machine.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 and its pawl pivot 42 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the input coupling remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in each release cable 46.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the input coupling remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in each release cable 46.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which displaces the release balance bar 48, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 no longer blocks the crank socket 38, and the operator inserts the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from the equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.
A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.
The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only load-holding features under a standing machine.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

# FIG. 1

A three-quarter perspective view of the whole platform standing on its support surface, seen from above and from the front left, so that the front and left sides are both visible. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.


A support surface 64 occupies the lower part of the drawing area as a wide horizontal slab in perspective, extending past the platform on the visible sides.

A base frame 10 rests on the upper face of the support surface 64. It is a closed rectangular frame drawn as a low box in perspective, its front and left walls visible as solid faces, shown schematically.

Four upright guide towers 14 rise from the base frame 10, one near each of its corners. Each guide tower 14 is a tall hollow upright column of the same height, its lower end joined to the base frame 10, shown schematically. The two rear guide towers 14 are partly occluded by the two front ones.

An equipment deck 12 is a flat rectangular slab held above the upper ends of the guide towers 14 and parallel to the base frame 10, shown schematically.

Four corner posts 16 depend from the corners of the underside of the equipment deck 12 and run vertically down into the four guide towers 14. A removable cover 60 is a plain rectangular panel lying flat against a wall of the base frame 10 between two of the guide towers 14, shown schematically.

A release handle 52 is an elongated straight lever projecting outward from a wall of the base frame 10, its inner end meeting that wall and its outer end free, shown schematically. The release handle 52 is shown in its pulled position.

A hand crank 36 is drawn as a short horizontal shaft entering a wall of the base frame 10, a radial arm at the outer end of that shaft, and a short grip parallel to the shaft at the far end of the arm, shown schematically. The hand crank 36 is shown in place in the platform.

content.content:
Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.
The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only load-holding features under a standing machine.


With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the locking pawls 40 remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in at least one of the release cables 46, and in the illustrated arrangement in each of them.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.


After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.
A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.
The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only load-holding features under a standing machine.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the locking pawls 40 remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in at least one of the release cables 46, and in the illustrated arrangement in each of them.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which displaces the release balance bar 48, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 no longer blocks the crank socket 38, and the operator inserts the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: All nine findings are fixed. FIG. 2 now places each rack on the fore-or-aft interior-facing side of its corner post and takes section line 4-4 on a front-to-rear cutting plane with both arrows pointing left, and the pinion is drawn as a wheel seen edge-on across its transverse shaft, so the sheet no longer implies a rack face or a pinion axis that the transverse-shaft drive cannot mesh with; FIG. 4 is unchanged and is correct under that viewing direction. The description now confirms the flags after the release handle has been released and before loading the deck, matching the interlock paragraph, the method paragraph and claim 18. The synchronizing transmission is defined once as the two transverse shafts plus the sprockets and chain, and claims 4 and 5 recite the shafts inside the transmission, so the term has one scope in the claims and the description. The pawl pivot is out of the load path in claim 13 and the description, the cover's mounting location is out of claim 21 and FIG. 1, the input coupling is out of the access list, FIG. 5 no longer adds an unnumbered support or a stated pivot spacing, the cable adjuster is recited for at least one release cable with the four-adjuster arrangement kept as the illustrated one, and FIG. 6 shows the hand crank inserted in the socket in both its view sentence and its body. The numeral table is unchanged, the abstract remains 139 words, and every figure brief is well under the character limit.
reasoning: The rack orientation was the finding with real mechanical content, so I fixed it at the source rather than at the section view. A pinion fixed to a transverse shaft turns about the transverse axis and can only drive a rack whose teeth face fore-and-aft, so FIG. 2 now says the rack sits on the rear-facing side of each lower post and the front-facing side of each upper post, and line 4-4 runs front to rear with both arrows toward the left. With that viewing direction the right wall band of FIG. 4 is the interior-facing tower wall, so the section sheet needed no change at all.

I also changed how the pinion is depicted in FIG. 2, because a toothed circle drawn in a plan view reads as a wheel spinning about a vertical axis and would have reintroduced the same conflict from the other side. Drawing it as a wheel seen edge-on, a short bar across the shaft running front to rear with one end at the rack, is the correct projection of the disclosed arrangement and adds nothing to the invention.

The flag-confirmation order was a genuine contradiction inside the document: the interlock holds the handle pulled until the crank is out, the pawls only re-seat when the handle returns, so no flag can appear while the crank is in the socket. The disclosure's own sequence puts confirmation last, and the description now says so, which also aligns it with the method paragraph and claim 18.

The transmission definition had drifted into two scopes, and the claims were the reason it mattered: claims 2 and 16 already treated a transverse shaft as part of the transmission while claims 4 and 5 recited the shafts as separate additions. I picked the inclusive definition, since under the narrow one the two pinions on a shaft are coupled by the shaft rather than by the transmission, which contradicted the sentence that immediately followed. Claims 4 and 5 now recite the shafts, sprockets and chain, or the shafts and the belt or gear train, all as parts of the transmission, so the term has a single meaning everywhere.

For the untraced items I removed the addition and kept the disclosed core. The pivot stays as the mounting that lets the pawl swing, which is inherent, but is no longer recited as a load-carrying member in claim 13 or the description. The cover stays as a removable cover giving service access, without a stated mounting on the base frame in claim 21 or a position between two towers in FIG. 1. The access list returns to the disclosed items, with the locking pawls in place of the input coupling. FIG. 5 loses the unnumbered support and the pivot spacing while keeping the bar mounted on the base frame and the handle joined at pivot 50, which is still enough to depict both the claimed mounting and the relative pivoting.

Claim 10 moved from a cable adjuster in each release cable to one in at least one of them, which is the safer recitation given that the source names cable adjusters only collectively, and the description keeps the four-adjuster case expressly as the illustrated arrangement so FIG. 5 and method claim 21 both remain supported.
