The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.
A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.

The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only members holding that load.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt running over toothed pulleys fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the locking pawls 40 remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in at least one of the release cables 46, and in the illustrated arrangement in each of them.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which displaces the release balance bar 48, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 no longer blocks the crank socket 38, and the operator inserts the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from the equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: Three corrections. The belt variant no longer recites toothed pulleys or their mounting: claim 5 and the corresponding description paragraph now say a toothed belt coupling the front transverse shaft to the rear transverse shaft, parallel to the gear-train alternative in the same sentence. The FIG. 2 rack paragraph now shows the rack as a short toothed edge appearing end-on in the plan view, with the rack stated to extend vertically along the corner post in the direction of travel, so the sheet agrees with the description and with the full-height rack of FIG. 4. Claim 19 now recites inserting the hand crank into the crank socket and turning the hand crank, so the dependent step actually performs the turning step of claim 17 that it narrows, matching the method paragraph of the description. Nothing else changed: the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the other five figure briefs, and the remaining claims are untouched and remain synchronized, and the abstract is unchanged.
reasoning: For the belt variant I deleted the added structure rather than trying to justify it. The disclosure substitutes a toothed belt for the endless chain and says nothing about pulleys or what they are fixed to, so claim 5 now recites the belt as coupling the two transverse shafts, exactly the phrasing already used for the gear train in the same claim. Scope is unaffected in practice, because any belt drive between those shafts still reads on the claim, and the claim no longer carries a connection statement the source never makes.

The FIG. 2 rack instruction was internally wrong for a plan view: a rack running vertically along the post cannot show a horizontal row of teeth when seen from straight above. Describing it as a short toothed edge seen end-on, with the vertical extent stated explicitly, keeps the disclosed direction of travel, keeps the face identified by the pinion it confronts, and stays consistent with FIG. 4, where the rack runs the full sectioned height of the post.

Claim 19 as written substituted insertion for turning, so it did not narrow the step of claim 17 it referred to. Adding the act of turning the hand crank fixes that without changing what the claim covers, since the interlock limitations on insertion and on handle return are unchanged, and it matches the description's method paragraph, which recites both acts in order.

No other file needed to move. The drawing descriptions do not mention pulleys or tooth rows, the numeral table is unaffected, and the FIG. 4 recitation of a row of teeth of constant pitch is correct there because that view is a vertical section along the post.

Claim 1 still rests on the synchronizing transmission moving every post by the same distance from one rotary input, the independent spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower, and the release balance bar pivotable relative to the release handle so a difference in effective cable length is taken up by the bar rather than leaving one pawl engaged. Claim 14 still rests on the two-way crank interlock together with per-pawl flags visible only at full tooth engagement, and claim 17 on the operator sequence those features enforce. input.summary: Two figure-brief corrections, neither touching the application text. FIG. 3 no longer claims to be seen in the same viewing direction as FIG. 2; it is now stated as a schematic diagram in which the two transverse shafts, the sprockets, the chain loop, the worm wheel and the worm input shaft are laid out diagrammatically in one plane rather than in a single projection, which is consistent with the sprockets and worm wheel drawn as circles and the chain drawn as a closed loop. FIG. 2's rack paragraph no longer gives two incompatible instructions: the rack is drawn as a short plain band on the interior-facing side of each corner post that confronts the pinion, with the rack extending vertically along the post in the direction of travel so its teeth are not resolved in a straight-down view. FIG. 4 keeps the full-height tooth row, which is correct in a vertical section. The claims, detailed description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table and the other four figure briefs are unchanged and remain synchronized.
reasoning: FIG. 3 had claimed a projection it could not have. Sprockets and a worm wheel fixed to horizontal transverse shafts lie in vertical planes, and the chain loop runs in that same vertical plane, so a straight-down view cannot show all of them as circles and a loop while showing the shafts as long lines. Declaring the sheet a diagram laid out in one plane rather than a single projection keeps every disclosed relationship the sheet exists to show, the sprocket on each shaft, the one endless chain coupling them, and the worm meshing the worm wheel on the front shaft, and drops only the false projection claim. The body of the brief and the Brief Description entry needed no change.

The FIG. 2 rack instruction was self-cancelling: a serrated edge drawn along the post in a plan view depicts teeth pitched horizontally, which contradicts the same sentence's statement that the rack runs vertically in the direction of travel, and contradicts FIG. 4. Drawing the rack as a plain band on that face keeps what the plan view is there to establish, which side of the post carries the rack and that it confronts the pinion at that tower, and leaves the tooth row to the sectional sheet where it can be shown truthfully.

Neither fix touched the invention. The description still says only that the rack extends along the corner post in the direction of travel and lies along an inward-facing side, claim 6 remains shape-neutral, and no numeral, part, or relationship was added or removed, so the numeral table and the drawing descriptions stayed as they were.

Claim 1 still rests on the synchronizing transmission moving every post by the same distance from one rotary input, the independent spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower, and the release balance bar pivotable relative to the release handle so a difference in effective cable length is taken up by the bar rather than leaving one pawl engaged. Claim 14 still rests on the two-way crank interlock together with per-pawl flags visible only at full tooth engagement, and claim 17 on the operator sequence those features enforce. This turn changed only two sentences in two figure briefs, so no claim scope, no described embodiment, and no fallback in the ladder moved.

input.summary: Three corrections, all internal-consistency items. The Brief Description now calls FIG. 3 a schematic diagram, matching the FIG. 3 brief, which lays the transmission out diagrammatically in one plane rather than in a single projection. The release handle is now described consistently across sheets: FIG. 1 shows the visible portion running outward from a wall of the base frame to a free outer end with its inner end concealed within the base frame, so it no longer terminates at the wall, while FIG. 5 continues to show the inner end meeting the release balance bar at the balance bar pivot. The cross grip on the release handle is deleted from FIG. 5, so the same numbered part ends at a free outer end on both sheets and no undisclosed grip structure is depicted. No claim, description passage, numeral, or other figure brief was changed, and the numeral lists, drawing descriptions and application text remain synchronized.
reasoning: The FIG. 3 mismatch was a naming leftover: a detail view is a projection, and that brief expressly disclaims one. Renaming the entry in the Brief Description resolves it in the direction the brief already established, and it matches how FIG. 5 is named in both places. The figure brief itself needed no change, and nothing about the disclosed sprockets, chain and worm drive moved.

The handle's inner end had two mutually exclusive specifications. I kept the one that carries the mechanism, the inner end meeting the balance bar at pivot 50 in FIG. 5 and in the description, and fixed FIG. 1 to show only what a perspective view of the assembled platform can show: the visible outer portion emerging from the wall, with the inner end concealed inside the frame. That keeps the handle a single part with a single connection across the set.

For the outer end I deleted the grip rather than adding one to FIG. 1, because the disclosure describes the release handle only as something the operator pulls and holds and never gives it a shape or a grip. FIG. 1's plain lever was already the generic outline adopted for this part, so removing the grip from FIG. 5 makes the two sheets agree without inventing structure.

input.summary: Two corrections, both confined to the FIG. 3 brief. The chain paragraph no longer fixes a routing topology: it now reads as one endless closed loop passing around the front sprocket and the rear sprocket and coupling them, shown schematically, with the outside-wrap and left and right straight-run language deleted, so the sheet no longer asserts an uncrossed loop or a common rotational sense for the two transverse shafts. The worm input shaft now ends in a short irregular break line rather than a free end, using the same truncation convention already applied to both transverse shafts on that sheet, so the shaft reads as continuing to the crank socket that the description and claim 16 couple to it. The application text was not touched, since the description and claim 4 already speak only of a chain running over the two sprockets and constraining the shafts to rotate through the same angle. Claims, description, drawing descriptions, numeral table and the other five figure briefs are unchanged and remain synchronized.
reasoning: Chain routing is a torque-path statement, not an outline convention, so the fix was to remove it rather than to pick the other topology. The disclosure says only that a sprocket on each shaft and one endless chain couple the shafts so all four pinions rotate together, which fixes equal motion and says nothing about sense. Leaving the loop routing-neutral also removes the conflict with FIG. 2, where each pinion sits inboard of the inward-facing rack it meshes, and it keeps the specification untouched because both the description and claim 4 are already direction-neutral.

I kept the statement that the rear sprocket lies in the plane of the chain loop with the front sprocket, because coplanarity is what makes a single loop around both physically possible and it says nothing about which way either shaft turns.

The free end on the worm input shaft asserted a terminated shaft exactly where the description couples the crank socket to it and where a motor may drive it. Closing it with a break line is the convention the same sheet already uses for the two transverse shafts, so the shaft is shown as truncated by the figure boundary rather than as ending there, and no end structure is introduced.

figures/FIG-3.md, worm input shaft paragraph: 'its lower end free' replaced by 'a short irregular break line closing its lower end'; the barrel shape representing the worm and its mesh with the worm wheel 34 are unchanged.

Claim 1 still rests on the synchronizing transmission moving every post by the same distance from one rotary input, the independent spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower, and the release balance bar pivotable relative to the release handle so a difference in effective cable length is taken up by the bar rather than leaving one pawl engaged. Claim 4 remains the chain-and-sprocket fallback and stays direction-neutral, reciting one endless synchronizing chain running over the front and rear sprockets, which is what the disclosure supports and is broader than any particular routing. Claim 14 still rests on the two-way crank interlock together with per-pawl flags visible only at full tooth engagement, and claim 17 on the operator sequence. This turn changed two depiction sentences in one figure brief, so no claim scope, described embodiment, or fallback moved.

input.summary: Two wording corrections, neither adding nor removing subject matter. FIG. 2 is now described, in both the Brief Description and the figure brief, as a plan view of the platform with the equipment deck omitted for clarity, so the caption no longer implies that removing the deck would take the corner posts with it while the sheet still shows those posts in the guide towers. The load-path clause of claim 1 now reads that the load of the equipment deck at each post is carried through the locking pawl carried by the guide tower in which that post slides, with that locking pawl in the locked position, and through that guide tower, which gives every referential term an antecedent inside the clause and matches the tying used in claims 7 and 13. Claims 2 through 21, the description, the numeral table and the other five figure briefs are unchanged and remain synchronized.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 caption problem was a word choice, not a depiction problem: the sheet correctly shows the towers, posts, racks, pinions and shafts looking down past the deck, and the description has the deck carrying posts that depend from it. Saying the deck is omitted for clarity states what the view does without asserting a disassembly that would carry the posts away, and I made the substitution identically in both files so the two cannot drift apart.

In claim 1 the spring element referred to 'that guide tower' before any tower had been designated within the clause. Tying the pawl to the tower in which the recited post slides supplies the antecedent from the elements already recited, and it uses the same construction as claim 7 ('the post sliding in that guide tower') and claim 13 ('the guide tower carrying that locking pawl'), so the claim set now reads consistently.

The amendment leaves scope untouched. The load still runs from the post through its engaged pawl and into the tower that carries that pawl, which is what the disclosure states, and no limitation was added, dropped, or narrowed. Because claim 1's substance did not change, claims 2 through 21 and the corresponding description passage needed no edit.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.
A removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.

The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only members holding that load.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the locking pawls 40 remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in at least one of the release cables 46, and in the illustrated arrangement in each of them.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12. To change the height, the operator pulls and holds the release handle 52, which displaces the release balance bar 48, tensions the four release cables 46, and moves all four locking pawls 40 clear of the four racks 18. With the release handle 52 held in the pulled position, the mechanical interlock 58 no longer blocks the crank socket 38, and the operator inserts the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38. The operator turns the hand crank 36, which turns the worm input shaft 32, the worm wheel 34, the front transverse shaft 22, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the rear transverse shaft 24, and the four pinions 20, and so raises or lowers the four corner posts 16 by the same distance, the equipment deck 12 remaining parallel to the base frame 10 throughout the height change.

When the desired height of the equipment deck 12 is reached, the operator removes the hand crank 36 from the crank socket 38, which frees the release handle 52, and then releases the release handle 52. The four compression springs 44 return the four locking pawls 40 into engagement with the nearest teeth of the four racks 18. The operator then confirms that the locked-state flag 54 of every locking pawl 40 is visible through the window 56 of the corresponding guide tower 14, and the machine on the equipment deck 12 is thereafter supported through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14.

Further embodiments

The four guide towers 14 near the corners of a rectangular base frame 10 with four corner posts 16 depending from the equipment deck 12 are one arrangement. In other embodiments the platform has three guide towers 14, or more than four guide towers 14, with one guided post sliding in each guide tower 14 and with one rack 18, one pinion 20, one locking pawl 40 biased by one compression spring 44, one release cable 46, and one locked-state flag 54 at each guided post. The synchronizing transmission then couples the pinions 20 of all of the guide towers 14, and the release balance bar 48 carries one anchorage for each release cable 46 and remains pivotable relative to the release handle 52 so that the same equalization is obtained over the number of locking pawls 40 present. The synchronized drive, the independent locking pawl load locks, the equalizing release balance bar 48, the interlock between the hand crank 36 and the release handle 52, and the visible confirmation of every engaged locking pawl 40 are unchanged by the number of guided posts.

The rotary input may be the worm input shaft 32 with the worm wheel 34 turned by the hand crank 36, or the same worm input shaft 32 turned by a motor.

The platform is reusable, and the worm drive, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the locking pawls 40, and the cable adjusters 62 are accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

The foregoing describes embodiments of the platform. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another embodiment where the two are not mutually exclusive, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: Two wording repairs, neither adding nor removing subject matter. Claims 14 and 18 now tie the flag, the window and the pawl together the way claim 7 already did: the window of each guide tower is positioned so that the locked-state flag of the locking pawl carried by that guide tower is visible through that window only when that locking pawl is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack of the post sliding in that guide tower, and claim 18 uses the same full tying, including the rack of the post sliding in that guide tower. In the Detailed Description, the removable cover sentence is now its own paragraph introduced by a reference to FIG. 1, the sheet on which numeral 60 appears, instead of sitting under the direction to FIG. 2. Everything else is unchanged: the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, all six figure briefs including FIG. 2's numeral list of 10, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22 and 24, the remaining claims and the abstract.
reasoning: Claims 14 and 18 recited plural flags, windows and pawls in one element and then referred back with bare definite articles, so nothing designated which flag belonged with which window. Adopting claim 7's construction supplies those designations from elements already recited, and it makes the three flag recitations in the claim set read identically, which is what an examiner comparing them would expect.

Claim 18 also lacked the tying of the rack to the post, so 'a tooth of the rack' had no single referent among the racks introduced in claim 17. Adding 'of the post sliding in that guide tower' closes that gap without touching the confirmation step, which already says the flag of every locking pawl is visible through the window of the corresponding guide tower.

Neither amendment changes scope. The relationship being claimed, a flag on each pawl visible through its own tower's window only at full tooth engagement, is exactly what the description and the disclosure state, so claims 7, 14 and 18 now say the same thing in the same words.

The cover sentence was sending a reader to FIG. 2 for numeral 60, which appears only on FIG. 1. Splitting it into its own paragraph under a reference to FIG. 1 fixes the pointer without moving the cover in the drawings or altering the access statement, and it keeps the practice used throughout this description of naming in a figure-referenced paragraph only parts listed on that sheet.

draft/09-claims.md claim 18: 'a window in each guide tower through which the locked-state flag is visible only when that locking pawl is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack' replaced by 'a window in each guide tower through which the locked-state flag of the locking pawl carried by that guide tower is visible only when that locking pawl is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack of the post sliding in that guide tower'; the confirmation step is unchanged.

draft/08-detailed-description.md: the removable cover sentence is now a separate paragraph reading 'Referring again to FIG. 1, a removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.', and the preceding paragraph now ends after 'the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.'
draft/07-drawings.md, draft/10-abstract.md, draft/numerals.md, claims 1 to 13, 15 to 17 and 19 to 21, and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md: unchanged and still synchronized.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and no claim was drafted against a document. Claim 1 still rests on the synchronizing transmission moving every post by the same distance from one rotary input, the independent spring-biased locking pawl in each guide tower taking the deck load into that tower, and the release balance bar pivotable relative to the release handle so a difference in effective cable length is taken up by the bar rather than leaving one pawl engaged. Claim 14 still rests on the two-way crank interlock together with per-pawl flags visible only at full tooth engagement, and the amendment sharpens that recitation referentially without narrowing it: the flag must still be visible only at full engagement, now tied unambiguously to the pawl and window of the same guide tower. Claim 17 and its dependents still cover the operator sequence, with claim 18 stating the confirmation step in the same tied wording.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	The draft is unusually faithful to its source. Every numbered part (10–64) traces to an exact passage of input/disclosure.md - base frame, equipment deck, guide towers, corner posts, racks, pinions, front/rear transverse shafts, sprockets, endless chain, worm input shaft, worm wheel, hand crank, crank socket, locking pawls, compression springs, release cables, balance bar, release handle, locked-state flags, windows, mechanical interlock, removable cover, cable adjusters and support surface - and the two structures the disclosure names only by function (the pawl's pivot and the handle/bar pivot) are directly supported by "a locking pawl that pivots" and "The balance bar can pivot slightly relative to the release handle." I found no numeral that labels two different parts: numerals.md, the detailed description and all six figure briefs agree on every one of the 28 numerals, and the union of the briefs' numeral lists covers all 28. The brief-description entries match the corresponding figure briefs item for item. I checked the FIG. 4 section geometry against FIG. 2 by hand: FIG. 2 places the front shaft at the bottom of the sheet (sheet-up = rear, sheet-right = +x), the 4-4 cutting-plane line is broken, runs front-to-rear through the lower-left tower, carries the designation 4-4 at both endpoints and an arrow at each pointing sheet-left, and is not listed as a reference numeral. Viewing along -x puts the rear (+y) on the right of FIG. 4, which is exactly where FIG-4.md puts the rack, the pawl space and the window - the two briefs are consistent. Showing the pawl in elevation on a plane that passes through it is the ordinary unsectioned-solid convention and the brief states it. The interlock logic is self-consistent across FIG. 1, FIG. 6, the description and the method (crank shown inserted only with the handle in its pulled position), and the confirmation step is correctly placed after handle release, matching the disclosure's own use sequence. Two limits on this review: no rendered-*.png sheets and no review/figure-audit-evidence.json exist in the workspace, so I could verify only the briefs, not pixels - this is the same gap the mechanical figure checks report. And prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references; the draft contains no [REF:] citation, so step 4 had nothing to check and the art of record is empty/possibly incomplete. My three findings are the generic recitations in the independent claims (the one substantive item), one overstated background assertion, and one term used three ways for the same element.

7	- **Every specification numeral appears in a drawing** (fail): 28 reference numeral(s) are used in the specification but absent from every drawing. Add each missing numeral to an appropriate focused sheet or redistribute the existing drawing plan. Do not remove a disclosed part, numeral definition, or supporting text to silence this check.

44	  - claim 19: “preceded”

46	## Reviewer findings
47	
48	- **[major] Independent claims recite generic drive input, spring and handle connection where every disclosed embodiment has only the specific species** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 14 and 17; compare draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶¶27, 29, 35, 41–43, 69) - Three recitations in the independent claims are genus terms whose only species in the disclosure is the specific structure. (a) Drive input: claims 1, 14 and 17 recite a bare "rotary input". The disclosure has exactly one input architecture - a worm input shaft driving a worm wheel fixed to the front transverse shaft - in both the crank form and the motor variant, and the candidate's own description defines the term only that way ("The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission"; ¶69 lists only the crank-turned and motor-turned worm shaft). As written the claims read on a platform with no worm at all, an architecture the source never presents and in which the disclosed back-drive resistance does not exist. (b) Spring: claims 1, 14 and 17 recite "a spring"; the disclosure and description use only a compression spring. (c) Claim 14 recites "a release handle connected to the locking pawls" with no balance bar or cables, reading on a rigid multi-pawl linkage, while the inventor states the "equalizing release balance bar" is present in every supported variant. Each generic term does read on the disclosed species, so this is a breadth judgment rather than a contradiction; I flag it because no disclosed embodiment lacks the worm, the compression spring or the balance bar, and the candidate's own description is the only place the generic wording appears.
49	  - Suggested fix: In claims 1, 14 and 17 replace "a rotary input" at its first recitation with "a rotary input comprising a worm input shaft and a worm wheel driven by the worm input shaft and fixed to a transverse shaft of the synchronizing transmission" (wording already present in claims 2 and 16 and in description ¶27), and recast claims 2 and 16 to the narrower disclosed detail, e.g. "wherein the worm wheel is fixed to the front transverse shaft". In claims 1, 14 and 17 replace "a spring" / "the springs" with "a compression spring" / "the compression springs" and delete claim 12 as redundant (renumbering the following claims), and make the same change in draft/06-summary.md ¶5 ("a spring biases each locking pawl" → "a compression spring biases each locking pawl"). In claim 14 replace "a release handle connected to the locking pawls" with "a release balance bar mounted on the base frame, a release cable connecting the release balance bar to each locking pawl, and a release handle acting on the release balance bar and movable to a pulled position...", and recast claim 15 to the pivotability limitation alone.
50	- **[minor] Background asserts a frequency ("the normal condition rather than the exception") that no source supports** (draft/05-background.md ¶9 (last sentence)) - The disclosure supports the existence of the failure mode - cable-length differences could leave one pawl engaged while the others release, which is why the balance bar is free to pivot. It does not support the stronger empirical assertion that in linkages of this kind the partly released condition is the usual outcome rather than an occasional one. There is no reference of record (prior_art/INDEX.md lists none) that could carry that characterisation either. The rest of the paragraph's reasoning (shortest connection lifts first, longest may not lift) is a mechanism explanation of the disclosed purpose and is fine; only the frequency claim is unsupported.
51	  - Suggested fix: Replace "make the partly released condition the normal condition rather than the exception" with "can leave one lock engaged while the other locks are released", so the sentence reads: "Where several locks are pulled by one linkage through separate flexible connections, ordinary differences in connection length can leave one lock engaged while the other locks are released, because the shortest connection lifts its lock first and the longest connection may not lift its lock at all."
52	- **[minor] The same element is called "post", "corner post" and "guided post"** (draft/04-field.md; draft/05-background.md ¶11; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶67; draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 14, 17) - The generic sliding member is named three ways. The claims and summary call it a "post"; the four-tower embodiment calls it a "corner post 16" (the numbered part, which is correct as a species name); but the field, the background and the further-embodiments paragraph call it a "guided post", which carries no numeral and is never defined as the same element as the claimed "post". Nothing is contradicted, but a reader tracing the ≥3-tower embodiment meets a fourth name for the element whose rack, pinion, pawl, cable and flag all carry numerals.
53	  - Suggested fix: Use "post" as the generic term everywhere and reserve "corner post 16" for the four-corner embodiment: in draft/04-field.md write "at each post"; in draft/05-background.md ¶11 write "every post of a deck"; in draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶67 write "with one post sliding in each guide tower ... at each post".
54

56	the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

Viewing along -x puts the rear (+y) on the right of FIG. 4, which is exactly where FIG-4.md puts the rack, the pawl space and the window - the two briefs are consistent. Showing the pawl in elevation on a plane that passes through it is the ordinary unsectioned-solid convention and the brief states it. The interlock logic is self-consistent across FIG. 1, FIG. 6, the description and the method (crank shown inserted only with the handle in its pulled position), and the confirmation step is correctly placed after handle release, matching the disclosure's own use sequence. Two limits on this review: no rendered-*.png sheets and no review/figure-audit-evidence.json exist in the workspace, so I could verify only the briefs, not pixels - this is the same gap the mechanical figure checks report. And prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references; the draft contains no [REF:] citation, so step 4 had nothing to check and the art of record is empty/possibly incomplete. My three findings are the generic recitations in the independent claims (the one substantive item), one overstated background assertion, and one term used three ways for the same element.

- **[major] Independent claims recite generic drive input, spring and handle connection where every disclosed embodiment has only the specific species** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 14 and 17; compare draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶¶27, 29, 35, 41–43, 69) - Three recitations in the independent claims are genus terms whose only species in the disclosure is the specific structure. (a) Drive input: claims 1, 14 and 17 recite a bare "rotary input". The disclosure has exactly one input architecture - a worm input shaft driving a worm wheel fixed to the front transverse shaft - in both the crank form and the motor variant, and the candidate's own description defines the term only that way ("The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission"; ¶69 lists only the crank-turned and motor-turned worm shaft). As written the claims read on a platform with no worm at all, an architecture the source never presents and in which the disclosed back-drive resistance does not exist. (b) Spring: claims 1, 14 and 17 recite "a spring"; the disclosure and description use only a compression spring. (c) Claim 14 recites "a release handle connected to the locking pawls" with no balance bar or cables, reading on a rigid multi-pawl linkage, while the inventor states the "equalizing release balance bar" is present in every supported variant. Each generic term does read on the disclosed species, so this is a breadth judgment rather than a contradiction; I flag it because no disclosed embodiment lacks the worm, the compression spring or the balance bar, and the candidate's own description is the only place the generic wording appears.

It does not support the stronger empirical assertion that in linkages of this kind the partly released condition is the usual outcome rather than an occasional one. There is no reference of record (prior_art/INDEX.md lists none) that could carry that characterisation either. The rest of the paragraph's reasoning (shortest connection lifts first, longest may not lift) is a mechanism explanation of the disclosed purpose and is fine; only the frequency claim is unsupported.
  - Suggested fix: Replace "make the partly released condition the normal condition rather than the exception" with "can leave one lock engaged while the other locks are released", so the sentence reads: "Where several locks are pulled by one linkage through separate flexible connections, ordinary differences in connection length can leave one lock engaged while the other locks are released, because the shortest connection lifts its lock first and the longest connection may not lift its lock at all."
- **[minor] The same element is called "post", "corner post" and "guided post"** (draft/04-field.md; draft/05-background.md ¶11; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶67; draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 14, 17) - The generic sliding member is named three ways. The claims and summary call it a "post"; the four-tower embodiment calls it a "corner post 16" (the numbered part, which is correct as a species name); but the field, the background and the further-embodiments paragraph call it a "guided post", which carries no numeral and is never defined as the same element as the claimed "post". Heavy machines are frequently installed above the surface that carries them. A rooftop unit may have to stand clear of a membrane, a shop machine may have to stand clear of a wash-down floor, and equipment carried on a vehicle bed may have to stand clear of the bed itself. When the required standoff height is not known until the machine is in place, or when the height has to change later, a fixed pedestal or a stack of shims is inconvenient, because setting or resetting the height means lifting the machine off the support again.

A height-adjustable platform avoids that lifting, but it introduces three problems that a design must solve together before such a platform can carry a heavy machine dependably.

The first problem is parallelism. If each corner of a deck is adjusted through its own screw, jack, or shim stack, the corners are adjusted one after another. The deck twists and cocks in its guides while the adjustment is in progress, the guided members bind against their guides, and the finished height at one corner differs from the finished height at another, so that the machine is left out of level and the guides are left preloaded.

The second problem is load holding. A drive train that both moves the deck and holds it is a single load path. Its gearing, its fasteners, and its input coupling all have to carry the standing weight of the machine for as long as the machine is installed, and any wear, backlash, or maintenance operation on that drive train is a wear, backlash, or maintenance operation on the only thing supporting the load.

The third problem is the state of the locks. Where a platform is held by separate mechanical locks, those locks must be released to adjust the height and must be returned afterwards. Two failure modes follow. A lock that is only partly released is dragged across the toothed member it engages while the platform is being adjusted, which damages the tooth flanks it will later have to sit on, and a lock that is never returned leaves the platform standing on its drive train while looking, from the outside, exactly like a platform that is locked. Where several locks are pulled by one linkage through separate flexible connections, ordinary differences in connection length make the partly released condition the normal condition rather than the exception, because the shortest connection lifts its lock first and the longest connection may not lift its lock at all.

There remains a need for a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform that changes the height of every guided post of a deck by the same distance from a single input, that holds the resulting height through load locks that are independent of the drive train, that releases every one of those load locks together despite differences in the lengths of the flexible connections that pull them, and that shows the operator, before the platform is loaded, that every load lock has in fact returned.

A reusable height-adjustable equipment platform supports a machine above a support surface such as a roof, a floor, or a vehicle bed while keeping an equipment deck parallel to a base frame.

In one aspect, the platform comprises a base frame carrying at least three upright guide towers and an equipment deck carrying a post for each guide tower, each post sliding vertically in its guide tower. Each post carries a rack, and each guide tower carries a pinion meshing with the rack of the post that slides in that guide tower, so that rotation of the pinion raises or lowers that post. A synchronizing transmission couples the pinions of all of the guide towers so that the pinions rotate together, and a rotary input drives the synchronizing transmission, whereby a single input rotation raises or lowers every post by the same distance and the deck does not rack in the guide towers.

In a further aspect, each guide tower carries a locking pawl mounted to pivot between a locked position engaging the rack of the post sliding in that guide tower and a released position clear of that rack, and a spring biases each locking pawl toward the locked position. The deck load at each post is carried through the engaged locking pawl and the guide tower rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone, so that the transmission is not the only load path under a standing machine.

In a further aspect, a release balance bar is mounted on the base frame and is connected to every locking pawl by a respective release cable, and a release handle pivots the release balance bar. Pulling and holding the release handle tensions all of the release cables together and moves all of the locking pawls to their released positions. The release balance bar is pivotable relative to the release handle so that differences in the effective lengths of the release cables are taken up by pivoting of the release balance bar and no locking pawl is left engaged with its rack while the remaining locking pawls are released. Releasing the release handle allows each spring to return its locking pawl into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack.

In a further aspect, each locking pawl carries a locked-state flag that is visible through a window in the corresponding guide tower only when that locking pawl is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack, so that the state of every load lock can be confirmed before the platform is loaded.

In a further aspect, a crank socket receives a removable hand crank that turns the rotary input, and a mechanical interlock associated with the crank socket blocks insertion of the hand crank into the crank socket unless the release handle is in its pulled position and blocks return of the release handle from its pulled position until the hand crank is removed from the crank socket. The interlock enforces an order of operations in which the locking pawls are clear of the racks before the platform can be driven and are returned to the racks only after the drive input has been disconnected, so that a locking pawl is neither dragged across a rack tooth during adjustment nor left released after adjustment.

In a further aspect, the rotary input comprises a worm input shaft and a worm wheel driven by the worm input shaft and fixed to a transverse shaft of the synchronizing transmission, the worm engagement resisting back-driving of the transmission by the deck load while the locking pawls carry that load.

In a further aspect, a method of adjusting the height of such a platform comprises pulling and holding the release handle to move all of the locking pawls clear of the racks, turning the rotary input to raise or lower all of the posts by the same distance while the deck remains parallel to the base frame, releasing the release handle so that each spring returns its locking pawl into engagement with the nearest tooth of its rack, and confirming that the locked-state flag of every locking pawl is visible through the window of the corresponding guide tower.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. Like reference numerals denote like parts throughout. Terms such as front, rear, upright, upward, and downward are used with reference to the orientation of the platform as it stands on a support surface, and are used for convenience of description rather than as limitations.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a reusable height-adjustable equipment platform comprises a base frame 10 that rests on a support surface 64 and an equipment deck 12 that is carried above the base frame 10 and remains parallel to the base frame 10 at every height. The support surface 64 may be a roof, a floor, a vehicle bed, or any other surface able to carry the platform and the machine mounted on it. The base frame 10 is a rectangular frame. The equipment deck 12 receives the machine it supports, and the machine remains on the equipment deck 12 while the height of the equipment deck 12 is changed.

The base frame 10 carries four upright guide towers 14, one near each corner of the base frame 10. The equipment deck 12 carries four corner posts 16, one depending from each corner of the equipment deck 12. Each corner post 16 slides vertically in a respective one of the guide towers 14.

Referring to FIG. 2, each corner post 16 carries a rack 18 extending along the corner post 16 in the direction of travel. In the illustrated embodiment the rack 18 lies along an inward-facing side of the corner post 16, that is, the side of the corner post 16 that faces the interior of the base frame 10.

A pinion 20 is mounted in each guide tower 14 and meshes with the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, so that rotation of the pinion 20 raises or lowers that corner post 16 and the corner of the equipment deck 12 attached to it.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a removable cover 60 gives access, on removal, to the synchronizing transmission, the locking pawls, and the cable adjusters described below, without removing the equipment deck 12.

A release handle 52 and a hand crank 36 are the members the operator handles, and the sequence in which they may be handled is enforced mechanically, as described below.

Synchronized drive

The platform comprises a front transverse shaft 22, a rear transverse shaft 24, and a worm input shaft 32, each mounted for rotation.

Referring again to FIG. 2, the two pinions 20 at the front of the platform are fixed to the front transverse shaft 22 and the two pinions 20 at the rear of the platform are fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24. Each of the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 extends from one side of the platform to the other, so that the two pinions 20 fixed to it rotate through the same angle.

Referring to FIG. 3, a front sprocket 26 is fixed to the front transverse shaft 22, a rear sprocket 28 is fixed to the rear transverse shaft 24, and one endless synchronizing chain 30 runs over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28. The endless synchronizing chain 30 constrains the front transverse shaft 22 and the rear transverse shaft 24 to rotate through the same angle.

The front transverse shaft 22, the rear transverse shaft 24, the front sprocket 26, the rear sprocket 28, and the endless synchronizing chain 30 together form a synchronizing transmission that couples all four pinions 20 for rotation together. Because all four pinions 20 rotate together, every corner post 16 travels by the same distance for a given input rotation, the equipment deck 12 rises and falls parallel to the base frame 10, and the equipment deck 12 does not rack in the guide towers 14 at any point during a height change, rather than being brought back to parallel after a sequence of separate corner adjustments.

The worm input shaft 32 carries a worm that drives a worm wheel 34 fixed to the front transverse shaft 22. Rotation of the worm input shaft 32 therefore rotates the front transverse shaft 22, and through the endless synchronizing chain 30 the rear transverse shaft 24, and through the four pinions 20 the four corner posts 16. The worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 form a rotary input to the synchronizing transmission. The mesh between the worm of the worm input shaft 32 and the worm wheel 34 resists back-driving of the synchronizing transmission by the weight on the equipment deck 12. The worm drive is not, however, the only load-holding feature of the platform. Under a standing machine the load is carried by the locking pawls described below, so that the worm mesh, the sprockets, the endless synchronizing chain 30, and the pinions 20 are not the only members holding that load.

The rotary input may be driven by a removable hand crank 36 received in a crank socket 38 coupled to the worm input shaft 32. The hand crank 36 and the crank socket 38 appear in FIG. 6. In another embodiment the hand crank 36 is replaced by a motor coupled to the same worm input shaft 32, the motor acting on the synchronizing transmission through the same worm wheel 34.

The endless synchronizing chain 30 running over the front sprocket 26 and the rear sprocket 28 is one form of the synchronizing transmission. In other embodiments the endless synchronizing chain 30 and the sprockets are replaced by a toothed belt coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24, or by a train of gears coupling the front transverse shaft 22 to the rear transverse shaft 24. In each case the transmission constrains all of the pinions 20 to rotate together.

Independent load locks at each guided post

Referring to FIG. 4, each guide tower 14 carries a locking pawl 40 mounted on a pawl pivot 42 fixed in that guide tower 14. Each locking pawl 40 pivots on its pawl pivot 42 between a locked position, in which the locking pawl 40 engages the rack 18 of the corner post 16 that slides in that guide tower 14, and a released position, in which the locking pawl 40 is clear of that rack 18 and the corner post 16 is free to travel. A compression spring 44 biases the locking pawl 40 toward the locked position, so that the locked position is the position the locking pawl 40 assumes in the absence of any applied release force.

With the four locking pawls 40 in their locked positions, the weight of the equipment deck 12 and of the machine on it passes from each corner post 16 through the engaged locking pawl 40 into the guide tower 14 and thence into the base frame 10 and the support surface 64. The four locking pawls 40 are independent of one another: each is carried by its own guide tower 14, is biased by its own compression spring 44, and engages its own rack 18, so that the standing load is carried through the four engaged locking pawls 40 and the four guide towers 14 rather than through the synchronizing transmission alone. The worm mesh, the endless synchronizing chain 30, the sprockets, and the locking pawls 40 remain accessible through the removable cover 60 without removing the equipment deck 12.

Equalizing release linkage

Referring to FIG. 5, a release balance bar 48 is mounted on the base frame 10, and four release cables 46 connect the release balance bar 48 to the four locking pawls 40, one release cable 46 to each locking pawl 40. Each release cable 46 runs from an anchorage on the release balance bar 48 to one of the locking pawls 40 and is arranged so that tension in the release cable 46 pivots that locking pawl 40 against its compression spring 44 toward the released position. A cable adjuster 62 is provided in at least one of the release cables 46, and in the illustrated arrangement in each of them.

The release handle 52 is connected to the release balance bar 48 at a balance bar pivot 50. Pulling the release handle 52 displaces the release balance bar 48 so as to tension all four release cables 46 and to move all four locking pawls 40 to their released positions, and the release handle 52 must be held in the pulled position for the locking pawls 40 to remain released. The release balance bar 48 is pivotable relative to the release handle 52 through a limited angle about the balance bar pivot 50. That freedom is what makes a single-handle release trustworthy at four separate locks. The four release cables 46 are flexible members whose effective lengths can differ from one another. If the release balance bar 48 were rigidly fixed to the release handle 52, the shortest release cable 46 would lift its locking pawl 40 first and would then absorb the remaining handle travel, and the longest release cable 46 might never develop enough tension to lift its locking pawl 40 at all, leaving one locking pawl 40 engaged with its rack 18 while the other three were released. That single engaged locking pawl 40 would then be dragged across its rack 18 as the platform was driven, and would resist the travel of the corner post 16 it holds. Because the release balance bar 48 can instead pivot slightly relative to the release handle 52, the pull is redistributed between the anchorages until every release cable 46 carries the tension needed to lift its locking pawl 40, and the difference in cable length is taken up as a small rotation of the release balance bar 48 rather than as an unreleased locking pawl 40.

Releasing the release handle 52 slackens all four release cables 46 and lets each compression spring 44 return its locking pawl 40 into engagement with the nearest tooth of the corresponding rack 18. No further action by the operator is required to lock the platform, because the locked position is the rest position of every locking pawl 40.

Visible confirmation of engagement

Each locking pawl 40 carries a locked-state flag 54 that moves with the locking pawl 40, and each guide tower 14 has a window 56 positioned so that the locked-state flag 54 is visible through the window 56 only when that locking pawl 40 is fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, as shown in FIG. 4. When the locking pawl 40 is not fully engaged with a tooth of the rack 18, the locked-state flag 54 is displaced from the window 56 and is not visible. The confirmation is therefore a confirmation of the position of the load-carrying member itself rather than of the position of the release handle 52 or of the release balance bar 48.

After the release handle 52 has been released and before loading the equipment deck 12, the operator confirms that all four locked-state flags 54 are visible through the four windows 56. A locked-state flag 54 that is not visible tells the operator, at the guide tower 14 concerned, that the locking pawl 40 there has not seated.

Crank and release interlock

Referring to FIG. 6, a mechanical interlock 58 is associated with the crank socket 38 and is coupled to the release handle 52. The mechanical interlock 58 blocks insertion of the hand crank 36 into the crank socket 38 unless the release handle 52 is in its pulled position, and blocks return of the release handle 52 from its pulled position until the hand crank 36 has been removed from the crank socket 38.

The mechanical interlock 58 thereby enforces the order of operations. The platform cannot be driven until the locking pawls 40 have been released, so no locking pawl 40 is dragged across a rack 18 while the platform is being adjusted. The release handle 52 cannot return while the hand crank 36 is in the crank socket 38, so the platform is not left with the locking pawls 40 released. Once the hand crank 36 has been removed, the release handle 52 is free to return and the four compression springs 44 seat the four locking pawls 40.

Method of use

In use, the operator places the base frame 10 on the support surface 64 and mounts the machine on the equipment deck 12.
